title: Your First Melody
description: Combine everything you have learned into your first real melody. Learn about phrasing, breath control, and musical expression.

tasks.title: What makes a melody?
content: A melody is not just a list of notes played one after another. A real melody has shape, direction, and feeling.

items: Shape - a melody rises, falls, and returns, like a sentence with a beginning, middle, and end
Phrasing - notes are grouped into short musical sentences, separated by tiny breaths
Emphasis - some notes are held longer or played louder to give the melody life
Resolution - a melody feels incomplete until it comes home to Sa

content.text: In Indian music, melody is everything. There is no harmony or chords - the entire emotional world lives in how you shape a single line of notes.

questions.prompt: Why does a melody feel 'finished' when it returns to Sa?

options.text: Because Sa is the loudest note
Because Sa is the tonic - the home note that gives a sense of rest
options.yes: Exactly! Sa is home. Landing on it feels resolved and complete.

options.text: Because Sa is the last note in the scale
options.why: Sa is the first note, not the last.

options.text: Because you always have to end on Sa
options.why: You do not have to, but ending on Sa gives the strongest sense of closure.

questions.prompt: I understand that a melody needs shape, phrasing, and resolution

hints: Think of a melody like a spoken sentence - it rises with a question and falls with an answer.

tasks.title: Breath between phrases
content: On the bansuri, your breath IS the music. Every phrase ends when you take a breath, and that breath is part of the melody.

items: Breathe at natural resting points, not in the middle of a musical thought
Take quick, silent breaths through your nose when possible
Let the last note of a phrase fade naturally before breathing
Start the next phrase gently, not with a blast of air

content.text: A common beginner mistake is running out of breath and gasping mid-phrase. Keep phrases short at first - 3 to 5 notes per breath.

questions.prompt: When should you breathe during a melody?

options.why: That would require impossibly long breath. Breathe at natural phrase boundaries.

options.text: At natural resting points between musical phrases
options.yes: Right! Breathe where the music naturally pauses.

options.why: That would chop the melody into fragments. Group notes into phrases.
Random breaths break the musical sentence. Place them deliberately.

questions.prompt: How many notes per breath is a good starting point for a beginner?
questions.yes: Good! Start with short phrases and build up as your breath control improves.

hints: Professional flautists can sustain 10-15 notes per breath, but they started with 3-5.
Quick nose breaths are quieter and faster than mouth breaths.

tasks.title: Play a short phrase
content: Start with the simplest melodic phrase: Sa Re Ga Re Sa.
This phrase goes up to Ga and comes back. It is a complete musical sentence - up, turn, home.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga Re Sa.

hints: Let Re be a stepping stone - do not linger on it. Ga is the peak, then come home.
Play it slowly enough that each note sounds clear.
Think of the shape: a gentle hill that rises to Ga and returns to Sa.

tasks.title: A longer musical sentence
content: Now extend the phrase: Sa Re Ga Ma Ga Re Sa.
This one climbs higher to Ma before turning back. Notice how reaching Ma adds more tension before the resolution.

questions.prompt: Play Sa Re Ga Ma Ga Re Sa.

hints: Ma is the highest point of this phrase - give it slightly more weight.
The descent from Ma back to Sa should feel like settling, like coming home.
If you run out of breath, take a quick breath after Ma before descending.

tasks.title: Adding weight to notes
content: Not every note in a melody gets equal time. Some notes are held longer to give the melody shape and feeling.
In this exercise, hold Sa for a full 5 seconds at the end of a phrase. Feel the resolution - this is what 'coming home' sounds like.

questions.prompt: Hold Sa for 5 seconds - feel the resolution.

hints: Let the note start gently and sustain evenly.
Close your eyes and listen to Sa against the drone. Hear them merge.
This sustained Sa is the resting point. Everything in a melody points toward it.

tasks.title: Call and response
content: In Indian music, a teacher plays a phrase and the student echoes it back. This is the oldest way to learn melody.
Listen to the phrase, then play it back. You will hear Sa Ga Ma Ga - then it is your turn.

questions.prompt: Listen and identify: which notes make up this phrase?
Now play the phrase: Sa Ga Ma Ga.

hints: Listen first, then play. Do not try to play along - wait for the full phrase.
The skip from Sa to Ga is the distinctive sound. Practise that leap on its own if needed.

tasks.title: A folk-style melody
content: Here is your first real melody, inspired by simple folk tunes played on the bansuri across India. It uses all the phrasing ideas from this room.

items: Phrase 1: Sa Re Ga Re Sa (the gentle opening)
Phrase 2: Ga Ma Pa Ma Ga (climbing higher, then returning)

content.text: Take a breath between the two phrases. Let phrase 1 end naturally, breathe, then begin phrase 2.

questions.prompt: Phrase 1: Play Sa Re Ga Re Sa.
Phrase 2: Play Ga Ma Pa Ma Ga.

hints: Master each phrase separately before connecting them.
Phrase 1 stays in the lower notes, phrase 2 rises. The contrast gives the melody direction.
Breathe between the two phrases - this pause is part of the music.

tasks.title: Rhythm and timing
content: Even without a tabla, your melody has rhythm. Each note takes a certain amount of time.

items: Long notes create a sense of rest or emphasis
Short notes create movement and energy
Even spacing gives a calm, meditative feel
Varied spacing gives a conversational, lively feel

content: In Indian classical music, rhythm is called 'laya'. There are three speeds:

items: Vilambit (slow) - for exploring and savouring each note
Madhya (medium) - the natural walking pace of a melody
Drut (fast) - for energy and excitement

questions.prompt: What is the Hindi/Sanskrit word for rhythm in Indian music?
questions.no: The word is 'laya'. Taal refers to the rhythmic cycle, laya is the tempo/speed.

questions.prompt: Which laya (speed) is best for a beginner practising a new melody?

options.why: Fast tempo hides mistakes. Slow practice builds clean habits.

options.yes: Correct! Slow practice lets you hear each note clearly and build muscle memory.

options.why: Medium is good once you are comfortable, but start slow.

hints: The saying goes: 'If you can play it slow, you can play it fast. If you can only play it fast, you cannot play it.'
Laya is the speed of the notes. Taal is the repeating rhythmic cycle.

tasks.title: The full melody challenge
content: Put it all together. Play this complete melody in three phrases, breathing between each one:

items: Phrase 1: Sa Re Ga Re Sa (open gently)
Phrase 2: Re Ga Ma Pa (climb up)
Phrase 3: Pa Ma Ga Re Sa (come home)

content.text: This three-phrase structure - opening, rising, returning - is the foundation of almost every melody in Indian music.

questions.prompt: Phrase 1: Sa Re Ga Re Sa.
Phrase 3: Pa Ma Ga Re Sa.

hints: Breathe between each phrase. The pauses are part of the music.
If a phrase is shaky, go back to that phrase's earlier task and practise it again.
Listen to the drone as you play. Each note should feel connected to Sa underneath.

tasks.title: What you have learned
content: You have just played your first real melody on the bansuri. Take a moment to appreciate what you can now do:

items: You know five notes and their fingerings: Sa, Re, Ga, Ma, Pa
You can shape notes into phrases with breath and phrasing
You understand resolution - the pull of every note back toward Sa
You played a complete three-phrase melody from memory

content: From here, you will add more notes (Dha and Ni to complete the scale), learn ornaments that make the bansuri sing, and begin exploring ragas - the melodic frameworks that give Indian music its infinite variety.

content.text: This melody you just played follows the basic structure of Raga Bhupali, one of the most beloved ragas in Indian music. You are already playing a raga without knowing it!

questions.prompt: Which raga uses the five notes Sa Re Ga Pa Dha (skipping Ma and Ni)?
questions.yes: Correct! Raga Bhupali (also called Bhoopali) is a pentatonic raga of pure joy.
questions.no: It is Raga Bhupali (Bhoopali) - a pentatonic evening raga full of serenity and happiness.

questions.prompt: I have played my first melody and I am ready for more

hints: Bhupali uses Sa Re Ga Pa Dha - no Ma, no Ni. It is a pentatonic raga.
It is often one of the first ragas taught to students.
